Crude oil prices bounced back in early Asian trade on Thursday, climbing higher after fresh reports of tankers hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz and the latest Yemeni Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia, which targeted a refinery.

At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $95.30 per barrel, with West Texas Intermediate at $84.36 per barrel. The rise follows several days of losses as traders focused on predictions of a supply overhang, ignoring the mine strike reports. However, the frequency of these reports, coupled with data showing the average daily flow of energy commodities out of Hormuz, seems to have broken through the glut wall, pushing prices higher.

Iranian state media reports of tankers hitting mines in Hormuz have become a daily occurrence recently, with some days seeing more than one incident, prompting tanker tracking firms such as Kpler to report a decline in daily average flows of crude out of the Persian Gulf. These reports are undermining the glut story, showing that exports of crude from the region are still—or once again—significantly lower than they were before the United States and Israel first attacked Iran at the end of February.

The Houthi attack on Ras Tanura, the largest refinery in Saudi Arabia, contributed to the change in trader perception, a reminder that there is a war in the Middle East and the prospect of peace remains quite remote. The Ras Tanura refinery is located on Saudi Arabia’s eastern coast, on the Persian Gulf, and is part of a major oil export hub.

“The broadening of the Middle East conflict threatens to halt the recovery in oil flows in recent weeks. Persian Gulf crude exports rose last week but remain on a declining trend,” ANZ analyst Daniel Hynes said, as cited by Reuters.

Energy analyst John Kemp, meanwhile, noted that global oil stocks had gone up in October but “the increase has been underpinned by a shuttle run and naval blockade of Iran organised by the United States that is very costly to enforce and may be unsustainable both financially and operationally in the medium term.”
